subject: psychiatry
title: Depression Rating Scales and Treatment-Resistant Depression

steps.tx: **Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression**, abbreviated HAM-D, is a clinician-administered 17-item rating instrument utilized as the international reference standard in clinical trials to quantify depressive symptom severity. Clinicians score items through direct interview and observation, yielding a cumulative score ranging from zero to 52.
steps.say: The seventeen-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale is the gold standard clinician-administered tool for measuring depression severity in clinical trials.

vis.title: HAM-D 17 Severity Stratification
rows: Full clinical remission target in trials
High symptom burden requiring intensive intervention

steps.tx: Trial reports need a shared severity number, which is what this card produces. The **Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression**, abbreviated HAM-D, is a clinician administered 17 item instrument used as the international reference standard for quantifying depressive symptoms. Items are scored from a direct interview and from observation, not from a form the patient fills in alone. The total runs from zero to 52. Sleep, mood, and bodily items therefore reflect what the rater elicits and sees, which is why the same card can compare patients across studies.
steps.say: The seventeen item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression is the clinician scored reference standard for depression severity in trials. The rater uses interview and observation, and the points add up to a total from zero to 52. It is not a questionnaire the patient completes alone.

vis.alt: A scoring card lays out the seventeen items of the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and groups the total into severity tiers.
vis.caption: Interview scores on the seventeen Hamilton items add up to a total between zero and 52, which the card then places in a severity band. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Treatment response and remission benchmarks** in clinical trials define therapeutic response as a minimum 50 percent reduction in baseline HAM-D score following therapeutic antidepressant intervention. Clinical remission requires achieving an absolute HAM-D score of seven or lower, reflecting complete restoration of psychological wellbeing.
steps.say: Clinical response requires at least a fifty percent reduction in HAM-D score. Complete remission is defined by an absolute score of seven or below.

left.title: Clinical Response
points: Fifty percent reduction from baseline score

right.title: Clinical Remission
points: Absolute HAM-D score of seven or lower

steps.tx: **Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors** serve as first-line pharmacological treatment for major depression due to superior safety, tolerability, and low toxicity in overdose compared to tricyclics. Common first-line agents include escitalopram, sertraline, and fluoxetine, which block the presynaptic serotonin transporter protein SERT to enhance synaptic serotonin.
steps.say: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first-line antidepressants with favorable safety profiles. They elevate synaptic serotonin by inhibiting the SERT transporter.

vis.title: First-Line SSRI Pharmacokinetics
rows: Purest SERT selectivity with minimal CYP interactions
Preferred in post-myocardial infarction cardiac patients
Longest half-life due to active metabolite norfluoxetine
Most potent anticholinergic & highest discontinuation risk

steps.tx: **Adverse effects of SSRIs** commonly include transient nausea, diarrhea, headaches, insomnia, and tremors during the initial two weeks of initiation. Persistent side effects encompass sexual dysfunction, including delayed ejaculation and anorgasmia in over 40 percent of patients, alongside risk of hyponatraemia due to SIADH.
steps.say: SSRIs cause transient gastrointestinal upset and headaches early on. Sexual dysfunction persists in many patients, and elderly individuals carry a risk of hyponatremia.

right.title: Long-Term Adverse Effects
points: Increased bleeding risk via platelet inhibition

steps.tx: **Treatment-resistant depression** is formally defined as failure to achieve clinical remission despite at least two consecutive trials of different antidepressant classes administered at therapeutic doses for adequate durations of 6 to 8 weeks. Clinicians must first verify medication adherence and rule out occult hypothyroidism, substance abuse, or bipolarity.
steps.say: Treatment resistance is defined as failing two consecutive trials of different antidepressant classes for six to eight weeks each at therapeutic dosing.

nodes.label: Confirm diagnosis, medication adherence, & exclude pseudoresistance
Screen for occult medical causes: TSH, B12, sleep apnoea
Switch to alternative class (SNRI, bupropion, or vortioxetine)
Augment with lithium, atypical antipsychotic, or thyroid T3

steps.tx: **Augmentation strategies in resistant depression** include adding lithium targeting a serum concentration of 0.6 to 0.8 mEq/L, or adding low-dose atypical antipsychotics such as aripiprazole or quetiapine. Other evidence-based options encompass thyroid hormone liothyronine supplementation, esketamine nasal spray, or switching to the dual-action agent venlafaxine.
steps.say: Augmentation options include lithium, low-dose aripiprazole, quetiapine, or liothyronine. Esketamine nasal spray provides rapid relief in resistant illness.

steps.tx: Adding a second medicine is one branch once a proper antidepressant trial has failed. **Augmentation strategies in resistant depression** include lithium with a serum level of 0.6 to 0.8 mEq/L, or a low dose atypical antipsychotic such as aripiprazole or quetiapine. Other options with trial support are liothyronine, esketamine nasal spray, and a change to the dual action agent venlafaxine. On the same algorithm, switching sits beside these additions, and electroconvulsive therapy is the escalation when drug strategies are not enough.
steps.say: Resistant depression may be augmented with lithium at a serum level of 0.6 to 0.8 mEq/L, low dose aripiprazole or quetiapine, liothyronine, or esketamine nasal spray. Changing to venlafaxine is another supported choice. These additions sit beside a switch of antidepressant and, later, electroconvulsive therapy.

vis.alt: A treatment algorithm for resistant depression shows a switch of antidepressant, drug augmentation, and escalation to electroconvulsive therapy.
vis.caption: After an adequate antidepressant course fails, the pathway offers a different drug, an added agent, or electroconvulsive therapy. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Electroconvulsive therapy indications** identify ECT as the most rapidly effective intervention for severe treatment-resistant depression, severe psychotic depression, catatonic stupor, and acute life-threatening suicidality. Therapeutic efficacy consistently exceeds 80 percent, far surpassing pharmacological augmentation options in emergency psychiatric presentations where rapid clinical response is life-saving.
steps.say: Electroconvulsive therapy is the most effective intervention for severe depression, psychotic depression, catatonia, and acute life-threatening suicidality.

left.title: Primary Indications for ECT
points: Immediate high suicide risk and lethal intent
Severe psychotic depression with food refusal

right.title: Clinical Efficacy Profile
points: Response rate exceeds seventy to eighty percent
Rapid clinical onset within two to three sessions
Bilateral electrode placement yields fastest response
Right unilateral placement minimizes memory deficits

steps.tx: **Absolute contraindications to ECT** do not exist, though significantly elevated intracranial pressure carries life-threatening risk of cerebral tentorial herniation due to transient intracerebral pressure spikes during seizure induction. Recent myocardial infarction within three months, unstable cerebral aneurysms, and acute retinal detachment require meticulous cardiovascular stabilization.
steps.say: Raised intracranial pressure is a critical contraindication risking brain herniation. Recent myocardial infarction and cerebral aneurysms require careful medical clearance.

left.title: High-Risk Medical Conditions
points: Recent myocardial infarction within three months
Recent retinal detachment or unstable glaucoma

right.title: Safety & Anaesthesia Regimen
points: Intravenous induction with propofol or methohexital
Pre-oxygenation with one hundred percent oxygen
